section_1.title: The Mystery of Rotational Growth
section_1.content: Introduce the concept of 'growth' in the complex plane. Explain that while standard exponents grow along a line, multiplying by 'i' represents a 90-degree rotation. This sets the stage for how exponents can create circular motion.
section_1.example: Imagine a robot dog spinning in place; each time it moves a 'unit', it turns a bit. We show a vector rotating around the origin of a graph.

section_2.title: Visualizing Taylor Series (The Bridge)
section_2.content: Briefly introduce Taylor series as a way to represent complex functions as polynomial sums. Show the visual overlap between the series for e^x, sin(x), and cos(x). Emphasize that when we plug 'ix' into the e^x series, the terms separate into real and imaginary parts.
section_2.example: Use an animation where the curves of sin(x) and cos(x) 'merge' into the exponential function e^(ix) as the series terms are added.

section_3.title: Euler’s Formula: The Geometric Key
section_3.content: Present the formula: e^(ix) = cos(x) + i*sin(x). Explain this as a coordinate map where 'x' is the angle and e^(ix) is a point on the unit circle. This bridges algebra and geometry.
section_3.example: A compass needle where the base is (0,0); as the angle x changes, the tip of the needle traces the unit circle defined by (cos x, sin x).

section_4.title: The Beautiful Identity: e^(πi) = -1
section_4.content: Demonstrate what happens when we set x = π. Calculate: cos(π) = -1 and sin(π) = 0. Show the resulting point (-1, 0) on the complex plane. Explain why this is considered the 'most beautiful equation' for connecting five fundamental constants (e, i, π, 1, 0).
section_4.example: A character walks from the positive real axis (start) exactly halfway around the unit circle to the negative real axis (arrival at -1). It's a journey of 'π' radians.

section_5.title: Real-World Application: Signal Processing
section_5.content: Summarize how this formula powers modern technology. By representing waves as complex exponentials, we can easily process audio and radio signals.
section_5.example: A smartphone transforming a messy sound wave from a pet's bark into clean digital frequency data using the rotation logic of Euler's formula.

section_1.content: Introduce the concept of 'growth' in the complex plane. Explain that while standard exponents grow along a line, multiplying by 'i' represents a 90-degree rotation. This sets the stage for how exponents can create circular motion.
section_1.example: Imagine a robot dog spinning in place; each time it moves a 'unit', it turns a bit. We show a vector rotating around the origin of a graph.

section_2.title: Visualizing Taylor Series (The Bridge)

section_2.example: Use an animation where the curves of sin(x) and cos(x) 'merge' into the exponential function e^(ix) as the series terms are added.

section_3.title: Euler’s Formula: The Geometric Key
section_3.content: Present the formula: e^(ix) = cos(x) + i*sin(x). Explain this as a coordinate map where 'x' is the angle and e^(ix) is a point on the unit circle. This bridges algebra and geometry.
section_3.example: A compass needle where the base is (0,0); as the angle x changes, the tip of the needle traces the unit circle defined by (cos x, sin x).

section_4.title: The Beautiful Identity: e^(πi) = -1
section_4.content: Demonstrate what happens when we set x = π. Calculate: cos(π) = -1 and sin(π) = 0. Show the resulting point (-1, 0) on the complex plane. Explain why this is considered the 'most beautiful equation' for connecting five fundamental constants (e, i, π, 1, 0).
section_4.example: A character walks from the positive real axis (start) exactly halfway around the unit circle to the negative real axis (arrival at -1). It's a journey of 'π' radians.

section_5.title: Real-World Application: Signal Processing
section_5.content: Summarize how this formula powers modern technology. By representing waves as complex exponentials, we can easily process audio and radio signals.
